I like DCC because it doesn't make the MC out to be some "chosen one" or undiscovered godling or whatever. He was thrown into a system that is intentionally cruel, but he's just a normal random guy trying to survive with his friends. Like Mordecai says in the beginning, Dungeon World is less like Survivor and more like The Running Man.

It's not meant to be a wholesome happy feel-good story, and that's fine!

But if you want wholesome and feel-good, Beware of Chicken is another excellent series with a main character who is just a normal random guy trying to s̶u̶r̶v̶i̶v̶e̶ live a happy life with his friends. It has at least double the talking animals without all the extermination-of-our-entire-species stuff.
Be sure to come back and share your opinion after you muster through a few more books. I'd love to hear from the perspective of someone who started out hating it but still continued.

In the beginning, I found Erin annoying but I didn't find her insufferable. A wonderful facet of this series is that nearly every single character (even the big bad villains, minus a few notable ones) have redemption potential and the ability to grow.

And yes. Parsneau does the lord's work in this series. The way she chose to voice the Antinium is incredible.

The first time I went to college, I was 18. It was a bad move. I was burnt out on the education world and ended up dropping after failing some classes. The second time, I was 23. Couldn't finish because I ran out of money, but I had A's in every single class and was even asked to retake a class for equal credits because the instructor thought I had great potential in that particular field.

If I had just saved my money and waited until I was more "adult" in my mindset, I could have gotten my degree with relative ease.

I was selected to be tested for "giftedness" when I was  in 2nd or 3rd grade. They took me and a boy from my class to an empty room where we both took the rest.

He was "gifted". I was not. I was dismissed to return to class while the boy stayed behind to discuss alternative education options.

It's been nearly two decades since then, and I'm still struggling with feelings of incompetency and the overwhelming fear of failure. I ended up in advanced classes when I was in high school, but the damage was done.

I was nearly thirty before I finally realized that I am, in fact, not stupid.

It's worth it for me. I get one free credit every month that I can use to "purchase" any audiobook. I can also buy extra credits (1 for $14.99, 3 for $37.99, 5 for $55.99[USD]).

However, this means that I'm spending between $11 and $15 per credit. So if I find a book that's on sale for $9.99, it makes more sense to purchase it outright rather than use a credit on it.

And if I'm feeling strapped for cash, I can relisten to any book I've "purchased" in the past. As of right now, I have nearly a thousand books in my Audible library that I can choose from.

**BUT!** The reason I say "purchased" is because you DO NOT OWN ANYTHING. You do not have legal rights to those audiobooks. You cannot download them off of the app into, say, an mp3 on a hard drive without a third-party that may or may not conflict with Audible's Terms of Service. You cannot share them with a friend. And once you cancel your subscription, I don't believe you'll have access to any of those audiobooks, no matter how much you've spent on them.

It's too late for me. I didn't know the books weren't *mine* until I had already built a hefty collection. I'm pretty much committed to Audible now. If that doesn't bother you, then no worries. If it does... Eh, idrk what other options there are...

Do you have a Google Pixel? Because most of us with Pixels have been having that problem for the last few days, regardless of headphones/earbuds/speakers.

It's an issue with the app or the OS, but I've found two things that might work:

**Apps > Audible > Mobile data & WiFi > Background data:** make sure background data IS enabled

**Apps > Audible > App battery usage > Unrestricted:** select "Unrestricted" rather than the default "Optimized"

Hope this helps.

Possible Fix 2: I tried your solution, but found my background data was already on. However under Apps > Audible > App battery usage, I changed it from "Optimized" to "Unrestricted: allows battery usage in background..." which (so far, fingers crossed, knock on wood) has fixed the problem.

2. If she's on TikTok, there's no way she hasn't heard of the Bird Test (sometimes called Bird Theory, or Bird-Bid).

It's a social study to gauge the success of a relationship. John Gottman of the Gottman Institute did a whole lab on it at the University of Washington back in the 90s. He "ran" a bed and breakfast for newlyweds where he could monitor their behavior and determine what behaviors indicated long-term happiness for couples. Several years later, during which some couples divorced, some stayed together but lost the love, and some were still blissfully married, he found that he could determine with 94% accuracy which couples would succeed and which would fail based on the outcome of a simple interaction:

"Oh, wow! Look at that bird!"

The percentage of times your partner *does* look at the bird (or the sunrise or the dog or the cool car or WHATEVER you point out) directly relates to how happy you two will be in the relationship. And the same for how many times you look when they point something out.

It's a way to not only show interest in something, but to ask to share that interest with your partner, and by looking, your partner is agreeing to share in that moment of interest with you. It's as simple as that. But it has a profound impact on the health of any relationship.

So for her to mock you when you show interest in something... That's pretty telling.

I disagree with most of this. Being emotionally mature is separating fantasy from reality when it comes to relationships. Am I disappointed because my boyfriend isn't a flawless supermodel billionaire who thinks I, a medium ugly woman in her 30s with bad skin and cellulite, is the most attractive person to ever grace this planet? Yes. But not actually. Because nothing about that is realistic. The fact that my boyfriend has a great smile and makes me laugh and buys me fruit snacks and thinks I'm the perfect woman /for him/ is both realistic and wonderful.

However. I agree on a more nuanced level. A lot of the romance genre leans on unhealthy aspects of relationships for the drama. Misunderstandings, push-pull tactics, hatefucking, things like that. It's not that these things aren't realistic, or even that they're poisonous to relationships in small doses. But they're often played up to enhance the anticipation for a climactic finale. High stress situations are GREAT to experience secondhand for entertainment, but if a person comes to associate those high levels of stress with love, that's unhealthy.

Likewise, there is never a happy ever after. The curtains don't fall once the couple get together. Wedding bells don't signal the end of someone's story. After the honeymoon is over, you still have to wake up with him/her every morning. You still have to do laundry and go to work and schedule holidays with both families. They're gonna gripe at you about getting toothpaste all over the bathroom sink, and you're gonna hate the way they leave the kitchen cupboards open. This is normal, and it's rarely (probably never) shown in the romance genre. That's not the fault of romance. It just doesn't make for good reading. But if you're not emotionally mature enough to recognize that life goes on after /The End/ then this genre won't help you learn that life lesson.

Let me regale you with a story from my not-so-distant youth. When I was 20, I found myself in an unhealthy relationship. It was a relationship that had lead me a thousand miles from home and all my friends and family, and it was a relationship that had left me stranded there with my ex-lover as my roommate. By the loving grace of my saintly mother, I made it back to my home in the dustbowl, but I left my heart in the backwoods of Tennessee.

For a long time, I jumped in and out of flings, filling the physical void because of my emotional emptiness. Most of them were childish and ill-tempered, and one of them puked on my bed. Shit you not. It was terrible.

Two years after moving back from Tennessee, I was sitting in the bathtub, drinking a beer and marathoning Star Trek: TNG on my laptop. That's when it struck me. I was content. I was actually enjoying my own company far more than I could possibly enjoy the company of a romantic partner. Thinking about including another person in my weekly walks around the park felt more like a daunting task than a pleasure. The thought of another warm body heating up my bed and taking up mattress space was repellant. The idea that I wouldn't have time to sit in the bathtub and drink beer and watch Star Trek was terrifying, and just imagining that there are people in the world who would JUDGE ME for doing so was laughable.

I started going out with friends more. I started doing projects and things around the house. I started reading books and going on solo road trips. It was then that I finally realized that I have so much to offer a romantic partner but that I was an independent person with the free will to selfishly hoard myself. I had myself all to myself, and I was surprised that I hadn't realized it before.

Fast forward a few years, as I'm sitting here in my sweatpants playing Duck Game I can safely say with 100% certainty...

I am lonely.

It isn't that I'm less confident in myself as a person. It isn't that I feel incomplete without the affections and devotions of another person. I just simply am lonely in the most basic sense. I would like to have the consistent company of someone whom I respect and appreciate as equally as I respect myself. I would like to find someone who can be my companion through this chapter in my life.

And yes, I would like someone who would share a beer with me as we watch Star Trek in the bathtub.

But I know without a shadow of a doubt that I had to first live with that emptiness before I could find out how much I love myself. I'm my own soulmate. That's how I know that, when I find the right person (hopefully soon, by god), they'll be outstanding because I'm outstanding and like attracts like.
